nameStory: Micrasterias rotata gets its name from the Greek 'mikros' meaning small and 'aster' meaning star, referring to its beautiful star-shaped appearance. The species name 'rotata' means wheel-like or rotating, describing how this tiny algae looks like an intricate, symmetrical wheel when viewed under a microscope. Despite being called by its scientific name, some people refer to these stunning single-celled organisms as 'desmid stars' or 'wheel algae.'
description: Micrasterias rotata is a microscopic single-celled green algae that lives in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow streams throughout New England. This tiny organism is shaped like an ornate, symmetrical star or wheel, with intricate lobes and projections radiating from its center. Each cell is divided into two mirror-image halves connected at a narrow waist, and the entire organism is only about 0.1-0.2 millimeters across - far too small to see without a microscope. What makes this algae special is its incredible geometric beauty and perfect symmetry.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: Under a microscope, the cell appears as a perfect star or wheel with identical mirror-image halves separated by a narrow constriction in the middle

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green due to chloroplasts (the parts that do photosynthesis) arranged throughout both halves of the organism

idTips.label: Lobed projections
idTips.description: Multiple arm-like projections extend from the main body, each ending in smaller finger-like points that give it an ornate, decorative appearance

idTips.label: Cell wall texture
idTips.description: The outer surface appears smooth and glass-like under high magnification, with a firm, rigid structure that maintains the cell's intricate shape

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Measures roughly 100-200 micrometers across (about twice the width of a human hair), making it one of the larger single-celled algae you might encounter

habitat: Look for Micrasterias rotata in clean, slightly acidic freshwater environments like bog ponds, quiet lake margins, and slow-moving streams with soft water. It thrives in areas with low nutrient levels and often grows alongside sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants. In New England, you're most likely to find it in pristine mountain lakes, cranberry bogs, and undisturbed woodland ponds.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. This is an excellent time to find them as they start reproducing after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when photosynthesis is most active. Water samples from sunny, shallow areas will yield the best results.
seasonality.fall: Still present and active through early fall, though populations may begin to decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases.
seasonality.winter: Populations are greatly reduced but some individuals may persist in deeper, more protected waters where temperatures remain more stable.

funFact: Each Micrasterias rotata cell is actually an living work of art that rebuilds half of itself every time it reproduces - when the cell divides, each half grows a completely new mirror-image side, creating two identical star-shaped masterpieces from one!
confusionNotes: Micrasterias rotata can be confused with other star-shaped desmid algae, but its specific pattern of lobes and the number of projections are unique. Remember: rotata has a wheel-like appearance with evenly spaced 'spokes,' while other species might have more irregular shapes or different numbers of main projections.
contextualKnowledge: Unlike the plants most people are familiar with, Micrasterias rotata is a single-celled organism, meaning its entire 'body' is just one cell doing all the work of living, growing, and reproducing. This puts it in a completely different category from mosses, ferns, and flowering plants, even though it's green and does photosynthesis like them.
compareHints: Micrasterias rotata differs from its relatives by having a more wheel-like, regularly symmetrical shape compared to the more elongated M. truncata or the deeply divided M. radiosa. While M. americana tends to be broader and more shield-shaped, rotata maintains its distinctive spoke-like projections that radiate evenly from the center. The 'rotata' pattern is generally more geometric and regular than most other species in this genus.
